title: Krishna Restores the Yadava Kinsmen
story:
For years, in the city of Mathura, the name Yadava had meant exile. The Yadavas were the great family of the city, Krishna's own family, and under Kamsa's rule they had slipped away one household at a time — uncles, cousins, in-laws: the Vrishnis, the Andhakas, the Madhus, all of them kin to the child the tyrant had sworn to destroy. They went in every direction, into foreign kingdoms where they could be nobody's kin and nobody's target, and there they grew thin and grey, worn down by years of borrowed roofs and borrowed names.

That child was Krishna himself, though he had not grown up among them. As a baby he had been carried to safety in the village of Gokula, out of Kamsa's reach, and he had returned to Mathura only when he was old enough to end the tyrant's rule. Now Kamsa was dead, and Ugrasena, the father Kamsa had imprisoned, sat on the throne. And Krishna sent word to every corner of the earth: come home.

The old texts say he brought back all his own kinsmen and connections from every direction — the very people Kamsa's fear had scattered. They came as they had left, by twos and threes, dusty from long roads, their faces lined by the same years that had emptied the city. Some had been gone so long that the grandchildren they brought had never seen Mathura. They stood at the gates uncertainly, exiles returning to a home that might not remember them.

Krishna met them himself, his elder brother Balarama beside him. He honored each one, spoke to them as a kinsman, and comforted them in their weariness. He settled them in their own houses, the houses their families had abandoned, and gave them back what Kamsa's rule had made them flee — fields, cattle, jewels, everything. Whatever they had lost in those foreign lands, he restored. The verses say that protected by the arms of Krishna and Balarama, they obtained everything their hearts had desired for years.

Then the city began to breathe again. Courtyards that had stood silent filled with voices, and rejoicing that the years of exile had deferred broke out at last. Day after day the reunited clans gathered where they could see the young lord's face, and the sight of him, the texts say, was delight enough. Morning and evening they came to look at him, and the looking healed them. It is said that even the oldest among them — men who had fled in their prime and returned stooped — became young again in Mathura, their strength restored until they seemed as vigorous as the sons beside them.

There was no battle in this homecoming, no enemy struck down at the gate. The enemy had been fear itself, and fear had lost its power years before, quietly, when a baby was carried out of the city and grew up safe in another village while his kinsmen scattered across the world. What remained was the slower work: gathering the scattered, returning what had been taken, and letting a city that tyranny had emptied fill up again with the sound of family.

When the last of the exiles was settled in his father's house, Mathura was whole in a way it had not been since before Kamsa seized the throne. The clans were one again under one king. And Krishna turned with his brother toward the task that came next — a quieter one, owed to them as princes: their own education.
reflection: Krishna's restoration of the scattered clans is quiet compared to the battles around Kamsa's fall, but it is the real work of kingship: gathering rather than conquering, and healing the long damage of fear. The detail that even the aged grew young again suggests that returning home — and being welcomed by the one who sent for you — restores more than wealth.
next_story_tease: But there was a debt of another kind still to be paid: the education of the two brothers.
hero_scene: Grey-haired kinsmen arriving through the gates of Mathura with their families and bundles, while Krishna and Balarama stand together at the entrance to welcome them, the exiles' tired faces brightening at the sight of the two brothers.
visual_elements: Krishna and Balarama at the city gate
